title: Tension and fabric pull in Tunisian crochet
subtitle: Why Tunisian fabric curls at the edges and how to manage it
excerpt: Tunisian crochet fabric has a strong natural tendency to curl upward from the lower edge and roll in from the sides. This is caused by the asymmetric structure of the forward and return passes. Understanding the cause makes it possible to manage it through hook size, stitch choice, and blocking.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776.

glossaryTerms.definition: In Tunisian crochet, the pass worked from right to left in which the hook picks up a loop from each stitch and holds all loops on the hook simultaneously.
In Tunisian crochet, the pass worked from left to right in which the loops are worked off the hook in pairs, producing the row of vertical bars visible on the fabric face.
The tendency of Tunisian crochet fabric to curl upward from the lower edge. Caused by the different tension of the forward and return passes pulling on the fabric in opposite directions.

content.text: Tunisian crochet fabric curls because the
forward pass
and the
return pass
pull the fabric in different directions. The forward pass draws the fabric horizontal; the return pass draws it vertical. This imbalance creates a
curl
toward the back of the work at the lower edge. The standard response is wet blocking after completion, which flattens the piece and holds it flat as it dries.
What you need

items.name: Tunisian crochet hook (with a stop at the end)
items.note: Or a standard hook with an extension cable for wide pieces. The full-width pick-up demands a long hook shaft.

items.name: Spray bottle or basin of water
items.note: For wet blocking the finished piece flat

content.text: Hook size and the curl

Tunisian simple stitch calls for a hook two sizes larger than the yarn label recommends. A yarn that calls for a 4.0 mm hook uses a 5.5 mm or 6.0 mm Tunisian hook. This compensates for the tighter fabric structure that Tunisian produces: the pick-up pass locks the loops tightly, and a hook that is too small creates an extremely dense, stiff fabric that curls severely.
Managing curl during work
Work the return pass more loosely than feels natural. The curl is worsened by a tight return pass. Let the working yarn sit slightly slack as you work off the loops.
Work the last chain of each return pass into the top left-hand edge of the fabric (not into the gap above the last bar) to prevent the edge from pulling in.

Every 10 rows, lay the work flat and check whether it is curling more than expected. Very tight curl at an early stage means the hook is too small for the yarn weight. Switch up a hook size and see if the fabric relaxes.
Blocking Tunisian crochet flat
Wet the finished piece fully by soaking it in cool water for 10 minutes.
Roll in a towel to remove excess water. Do not wring.
Lay flat on the blocking mat. Stretch the piece firmly against the curl: it will resist. Pin all four edges and then the interior at regular intervals to keep the fabric flat.
Leave to dry completely, at least 12 hours. The piece will hold its flat shape after the first blocking, but may need re-blocking after washing.
Common problems

items.symptom: The piece curls back to a tube shape within days of blocking
items.cause: The fibre does not hold a blocked shape well (acrylic, synthetic blends), or the blocking was not thorough enough.
items.fix: Re-block more aggressively, keeping the piece pinned until bone-dry. For synthetics, steam blocking rather than wet blocking produces a more durable result.

items.symptom: The side edges of the piece are pulling in, narrowing the work
items.cause: The edge stitch on each return pass is being worked too tightly, drawing in the last bar of each row.
items.fix: On the return pass, do not work the last chain tightly into the edge bar. Let it sit slightly loose, then pin the edges firmly during blocking.

items.symptom: The fabric has a pronounced diagonal distortion rather than a simple curl
items.cause: The tension differs between the forward and return passes in a consistent direction.
items.fix: Consciously match the tension between the two passes. Swatch 20 rows and measure the degree of diagonal; if it is present, slow down on one pass and let the hook sit at a more relaxed angle.

content.text: What to try next

Work a 30-row swatch in Tunisian simple stitch at the standard hook size and at one size up. Block both and compare. The larger-hook swatch will have less tendency to curl and will block flatter with less pinning effort. This demonstrates the hook-size principle more clearly than any description.
